newsitem.title: USA: GM strikes will hamper market share goal.
newsitem.headline: GM strikes will hamper market share goal.

text.p: General Motors Corp Chairman Jack Smith said on Thursday that GM will not likely reach its goal of capturing 33 percent of the U.S. light vehicle market in 1997 because of strikes this year.

"I think we're going to do better than last year but obviously we're not going to be at the upper limits of what we thought we'd be able to do because of the strikes," Smith told reporters at a breakfast meeting at GM's new global headquarters here.
"It would be tough to hit the 33 percent number with the strikes," Smith said.
In 1996, GM's had about 31 percent of the U.S. car and truck market and had hoped that introductions of several new car models would reverse a long term market share decline.

But Smith said that the 7-week strike in Oklahoma City has sharply reduced supplies of GM's all new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass mid-sized models and added that GM cannot make up that lost production this year.
Smith said that the tentative agreement to settle the strike in Oklahoma City adds jobs to the plant but allows the Cutlass and Malibu to remain very competitive cars from a cost standpoint.

"I don't know if I could call it a gain, but we're still in line to have that car be competitive in the marketplace, Smith said adding that GM "pretty much" maintained the productivity gains associated with the new vehicles.
He said GM will have to spend more money to re-start the advertising launch for the Malibu and Cutlass but added that GM is "not going to go broke on it."
He said the recent local strikes are unfortunate but they would not deter GM from continuing to improve its manufacturing efficiency.

"I think we've got plants that aren't as competitive as they need to be. We've got a strong push to get those plants competitive. We believe it is absolutely necessary for the long term competitiveness of the corporation, and we're striving to get there," Smith said.
